rollups.text: Jamie’s stock-trading project technology stack, as discussed on 2024-03-01: Python 3.10, Flask 2.3.2, PostgreSQL 14 database `trade_data` on localhost with Flask-SQLAlchemy, and React 18.2. On 2024-03-16, Jamie also discussed Redis 7.0 caching, pytest 7.3.1, TA-Lib 0.4.24, TensorFlow 2.11, Docker Compose v2.12.0, and the Alpaca brokerage API; Jamie reported using Pylint 2.15.0 and Pandas 1.5.3 in project discussions. On 2024-03-30, Jamie continued using TensorFlow 2.11 for LSTM work and Docker Compose for service orchestration.

Jamie repeatedly worked with stock-market data sources and caching for the trading bot. On 2024-03-01, Jamie discussed Alpha Vantage intraday 1-minute data for AAPL and MSFT, Redis caching, and a target of 99.9% stock-price data availability. On 2024-03-16, Jamie continued Alpha Vantage integration for AAPL and MSFT, discussed failover providers including IEX Cloud or Yahoo Finance, and reported Redis caching with a 92% hit rate in load tests. On 2024-03-30, Jamie again worked on Alpha Vantage integration and Redis caching. Jamie reported rotating Alpha Vantage keys on 2024-03-14 and accessing the key through `ALPHA_VANTAGE_KEY` on 2024-03-16.

Jamie explored or worked with several machine-learning and trading approaches. On 2024-03-01, Jamie shared a RandomForestClassifier prototype and asked about alternatives including Gradient Boosting, SVM, Logistic Regression, and MLP; Jamie also discussed technical indicators and backtesting. On 2024-03-16, Jamie worked with SMA and RSI indicators using TA-Lib, asked about an SMA-crossover backtest and time-series cross-validation, and explored an LSTM trend-prediction model. On 2024-03-30, Jamie was training TensorFlow LSTMs for stock prediction, including an LSTM(50) with a Dense output and input windows of 10 or 30 timesteps.

Jamie’s autonomous stock-trading bot project progressed through several milestones and sprint plans. On 2024-03-01, Jamie said the bot was due that day and still had substantial work remaining; a separate planned sprint ran March 1–15, focused on API integration and data ingestion. On March 10, Jamie planned a first milestone to fetch and store 1-minute Alpha Vantage prices for AAPL and MSFT, calculate indicators, and keep ingestion memory below 150 MB. On March 15, Jamie reported completing milestone 1, having fetched and stored more than 10,000 price points in PostgreSQL. Sprint 2 was planned for March 16–29 to build ML training and backtesting, integrate both with ingestion, and test them. On March 30, Jamie said milestone 2—completing ML training and deploying the prediction API—was due that day, but reported inaccurate predictions. Elapsed time from the March 1 deadline discussion to the March 30 milestone report: 29 days; from milestone 1 completion to milestone 2: 15 days.

Jamie’s Alpha Vantage fetcher work repeatedly encountered missing response data and rate-limit concerns. On 2024-03-01, Jamie reported `KeyError: 'Time Series (1min)'`, discussed HTTP 429 retry handling, and sought 99.9% availability; the initial code used Alpha Vantage `TIME_SERIES_INTRADAY` at interval `1min` and lacked robust handling. On March 16, Jamie again reported the missing-key problem while fetching AAPL and MSFT with a 12-second inter-symbol delay, and sought retries, caching, failover, and controlled retry tests. Jamie later reported rotating keys on March 14 and using `ALPHA_VANTAGE_KEY`. On March 30, Jamie again reported an HTTP 404 during Alpha Vantage integration. Elapsed time from the first reported missing-key issue to the later HTTP 404: 29 days; the missing-key issue recurred at least across March 1, March 16, and March 30.
rollups.topic: Alpha Vantage fetcher errors, limits, and reliability

rollups.text: Jamie’s stock-data latency work showed measurable improvement. On 2024-03-01, Jamie targeted under 250 ms for stock-price API fetches and reported an API target for a Flask endpoint. On March 16, Jamie reported that reusing HTTP sessions reduced average API response time from 400 ms to 220 ms, then asked how to reduce latency further. On March 16, Jamie also sought a response below 150 ms for a separate `/api/prices` endpoint. Elapsed time between the initial 250 ms target and the 220 ms result: 15 days. The 220 ms result remained above the separate 150 ms endpoint target.
rollups.topic: API latency targets and measured change

rollups.text: Jamie’s Redis caching work developed from considering caching to reporting load-test results. On 2024-03-01, Jamie asked whether Redis needed separate setup and discussed caching stock prices for 60 seconds. On March 16, Jamie asked about local Redis setup and caching Alpha Vantage data; Jamie later reported using Redis 7.0 for the last five minutes of price data and a 92% cache hit rate in load tests, with keys formatted `price_data:{symbol}`. Jamie also expressed a preference for Redis over in-memory dictionaries because of scalability and persistence across service restarts, and asked about RDB snapshots. Elapsed time from the initial Redis setup question to the reported 92% hit rate: 15 days.

Jamie’s LSTM model work moved from model setup and input-shape debugging to training and deployment concerns. On 2024-03-16, Jamie explored a TensorFlow LSTM trend-prediction model. On March 30, Jamie reported training on 30,000 data points and a rank-2 versus rank-3 input error; later Jamie reported 50 epochs with batch size 64 and validation loss 0.032, while asking whether the model was overfitting or underfitting. Jamie also encountered undefined test variables, asked about saving the model for production, and continued debugging input shapes. On March 30, Jamie said the prediction API was producing inaccurate predictions near the milestone deadline, and asked about TensorBoard, learning-rate adjustment, and varying input sizes. Elapsed time between initial LSTM exploration and the March 30 debugging and deployment questions: 14 days.
rollups.topic: LSTM model training, debugging, and deployment

rollups.text: Jamie’s testing and coverage goals increased across sessions. On 2024-03-01, Jamie aimed for about 85% coverage of `fetcher.py` in the first sprint. On March 16, Jamie reported 88% fetcher coverage and asked how to cover remaining code; Jamie also reported about 95% code coverage while integration tests were troublesome, then described fetcher/database integration tests as passing at a 97% success rate as of March 17. On March 30, Jamie reported 90% coverage for ML preprocessing tests. The stated fetcher coverage goal rose from approximately 85% to 88%; the later 97% figure referred to integration-test success, not code coverage.

Jamie reported the `KeyError: 'Time Series (1min)'` problem on at least four distinct dates: 2024-03-01, 2024-03-16, and 2024-03-30, with multiple reports on March 1 and March 16. The recurring issue involved Alpha Vantage responses lacking the expected intraday time-series key; no final resolution was reported.

Jamie reported average API response time changing from 400 ms to 220 ms on 2024-03-16 after optimizing HTTP session reuse, a decrease of 180 ms (45%). Jamie also discussed targets of under 250 ms for stock-price fetches and under 150 ms for a separate `/api/prices` endpoint; no measurement confirming either target was achieved was reported.

Jamie’s reported memory-use figures included a target below 150 MB for ingestion on 2024-03-10, a reduction from 180 MB to 140 MB after fixing data-loader memory leaks on 2024-03-16, and a subsequent request for further reduction. The reported reduction was 40 MB, about 22%; Jamie did not report achieving the separate below-150-MB ingestion target with the earlier indicator pipeline.

Jamie planned a March 30–April 12, 2024 sprint to build backtesting and paper-trading modules, integrate them, and test the system (March 30). On April 13, Jamie was implementing a 20/50-period SMA crossover backtest on 50,000 historical data points, reported reducing runtime from about 12 minutes to 4 minutes through Pandas vectorization, and considered further profiling and optimization. Jamie also reported reducing peak memory from 3 GB to 1.2 GB by chunking data, while continuing to address memory issues. The work expanded to include SMA/RSI indicators, return and risk metrics, visualizations, paper-trade simulation, and a separate backtesting service planned for port 5001. By April 27, Jamie was still optimizing SMA backtests and working on risk management and paper-trading integration; completion of the broader work was not confirmed. Elapsed time from the initial sprint plan to the latest related records: 28 days.
rollups.topic: Autonomous trading bot backtesting and paper-trading development

rollups.text: On April 13, 2024, Jamie was planning paper-trading work for an April 13–26 sprint, including timestamped simulated-trade logs and integration of a 2% maximum capital risk per trade with a stop loss 1.5% below entry. Jamie shared a RiskManager implementation and sought help enforcing those rules; the sprint plan proposed refining position sizing, integrating risk rules, logging, and unit and integration testing. By April 27, Jamie said the paper-trading module was implemented but its risk-management portion was not behaving as expected, and shared a risk calculation based on trade amount, leverage, and stop-loss value. The assistant suggested comparing per-trade risk with 2% of total capital and considering aggregate exposure. Elapsed time between the initial sprint discussion and the latest reported issue: 14 days.
rollups.topic: Paper-trading risk controls and sprint work

rollups.text: On March 30, 2024, Jamie wanted Redis caching for ML predictions with a 30-second TTL and a target of 40% fewer repeated inference calls. The initial code stored results without checking the cache; later guidance recommended input-derived keys and cache lookups. On April 13, Jamie reported caching backtest results with a one-hour TTL and 70% fewer repeated computations, while seeking further optimization. On April 27, Jamie again reported the 70% reduction and asked about bottlenecks; the shared implementation created a Redis client inside the function and set expiration separately. The assistant recommended reusing the client and considering pipelining. Elapsed time from the initial caching goal to the latest report: 28 days.
rollups.topic: Redis caching and reported computation reductions

rollups.text: On April 27, 2024, Jamie reported several issues integrating the Alpaca paper-trading API: an `invalid api version` error, an `invalid endpoint` error from `list_positions()`, and a 415 Unsupported Media Type error while testing an order in Postman. Jamie planned to upgrade `alpaca_trade_api` and explicitly set API version `v2`; for the endpoint issue, Jamie said they would try the suggested checks and share details if it persisted. Jamie also reported that reusing HTTP sessions had reduced order-placement latency from 350 ms to 120 ms for `https://paper-api.alpaca.markets/v2/orders`. The conversation did not confirm that the API errors were resolved. Elapsed time between the earliest and latest related reports: 0 days.
rollups.topic: Alpaca API troubleshooting and order-placement latency

Jamie reported that Redis caching of backtest results reduced repeated computations by 70% on April 13 and again on April 27, 2024. Separately, Jamie set a 40% reduction in repeated ML inference calls as a goal for 30-second prediction caching on March 30; achievement of that goal was not reported.
rollups.topic: Reported and targeted computation reductions from caching

Jamie’s stated preferences: include accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score when discussing machine-learning model training (recorded March 30, 2024); include API response metrics when discussing API-integration performance (recorded April 13, 2024); and provide API endpoint URLs in API-integration answers (undated records).

Technologies and tools Jamie repeatedly used, considered, or discussed: Python (2024-04-27..2024-06-08); Flask (2024-04-27..2024-05-25); Alpaca API and paper trading (2024-04-27..2024-05-25); pytest (2024-04-27..2024-06-08); Redis (2024-04-27..2024-05-25); gRPC (2024-04-27..2024-05-11); Prometheus 2.44 and Grafana 9.5 (2024-05-11..2024-05-25); Elasticsearch and ELK (2024-05-11..2024-05-25); Celery 5.3.1 (2024-05-11..2024-05-25); React 18.2, Chart.js 4.3.0, TypeScript, and Redux Toolkit 1.9.5 (2024-05-25..2024-06-08); WebSockets (2024-05-25..2024-06-08); Twilio (2024-06-08); SQLite (2024-06-08); AWS Lambda and CloudWatch (2024-06-08).

rollups.text: Jamie’s React trade-monitoring dashboard underwent repeated load-time optimization. On 2024-05-25, Jamie reported that lazy loading Chart.js reduced load time from 3.5 seconds to 1.2 seconds. Jamie later reported 0.9 seconds after optimizations, while noting the statement was made May 25 but referred to optimizations dated May 26. On 2024-06-08, Jamie again reported a 3.5-second load time and a target below 1.2 seconds, after trying lazy loading and database-query optimization. The records therefore contain differing measurements; no final resolution of the June 8 target was reported. Elapsed time: 14 days from the first improvement report to the June 8 renewed optimization request.

Jamie’s alert escalation and notification system progressed from planning to implementation and troubleshooting. On 2024-05-25, Jamie planned an alert escalation and notification system for production deployment by 2024-06-07; proposed sprint estimates ranged from 47 to 116 hours, and Jamie separately allocated 18 hours to the notification system. On 2024-06-08, Jamie was implementing alert escalation in alert_manager.py, testing it with pytest 7.3.1 at about 95% coverage, and troubleshooting Twilio installation, SMS sender-number validity, SMTP authentication, database query overhead, and alert-processing latency. A separate Milestone 7 deadline was 2024-06-10; Jamie said some features were already implemented but did not specify which. Elapsed time: 14 days from initial sprint planning to implementation troubleshooting; the stated Milestone 7 deadline was two days after the June 8 status.

Jamie repeatedly addressed WebSocket reliability and lifecycle for real-time monitoring. On 2024-05-25, Jamie reported persistent disconnections despite changing heartbeat intervals and explored reconnection when server heartbeats were unsupported. Jamie also worked on a five-second reconnect interval and preventing leaks from unclosed connections; a separate report said fixing unclosed WebSockets reduced memory use by 30 MB, though performance issues remained. On 2024-06-08, Jamie asked for a five-second reconnect interval and help ensuring an asyncio WebSocket client closes connections correctly. Elapsed time: 14 days from the May 25 troubleshooting to the June 8 follow-up.
rollups.topic: WebSocket disconnections, reconnection, and memory leaks

rollups.text: Jamie’s monitoring and alerting work repeatedly involved a self-managed Prometheus and Grafana stack. On 2024-05-11, Jamie used Prometheus 2.44 and Grafana 9.5 for trade-execution and system-health monitoring, with a Flask API and PostgreSQL alert data; Jamie explicitly preferred Prometheus and Grafana over cloud-native monitoring for cost and control. Jamie planned monitoring and alerting features by 2024-05-24 and a monitoring dashboard and alerting system by 2024-05-30. On 2024-05-25, a later milestone plan included production deployment of alert escalation and notifications by June 7. Elapsed time: 27 days from the May 11 monitoring work to the June 7 planned deployment date.

Recorded latency and load-time figures across Jamie’s work: live-trading API latency was about 400 ms before persistent session reuse and later 180 ms, a reported reduction of 220 ms (55%) (2024-05-11..2024-05-25); the paper-trading module was reported at about 350 ms with a 120-ms target (2024-05-11); alert processing was reported at 500 ms with a 150-ms target (2024-06-08). Dashboard load time was reported as 3.5 seconds, then 1.2 seconds after lazy loading, and also 0.9 seconds after further optimization (2024-05-25); a separate June 8 report again gave 3.5 seconds and a below-1.2-second target. These figures describe different reports and targets, not a single verified continuous measurement series.

Jamie repeatedly raised API authentication and authorization security: on 2024-04-27, requests covered admin two-factor authentication, a 401 response, and token-validation network failures; on 2024-05-11, Jamie explicitly requested security safeguards for API integration and authentication/authorization answers; on 2024-05-25, Jamie discussed Alpaca OAuth, Auth0 role-based access control, and webhook authentication and authorization. Jamie’s standing preference was to include security measures when discussing authentication and authorization, and to include security protocols in API integration answers.
rollups.topic: Security preferences and recurring authentication concerns

Jamie’s autonomous trading-bot deployment and reliability work progressed from AWS and Lambda alerting and deployment planning (2024-06-08) to an EC2/Docker Compose connectivity problem and asynchronous API calls, SMS trade notifications, PostgreSQL trade storage, and container-memory troubleshooting (2024-06-22; 14 days after June 8). By 2024-07-06, Jamie reported the full stack running on AWS EC2 t3.medium instances with Docker Compose v2.12.0; a test of 1,000 trades over 24 hours had a 98% successful execution rate. Performance improvement remained an open goal (2024-07-06; 14 days after June 22).

A separate task breakdown totaled 20 hours, or 22 hours with a proposed buffer; to fit 16 hours, the suggested plan reduced testing and deferred documentation, but Jamie’s acceptance was not recorded (2024-06-08). Jamie then described a production deployment and load-testing milestone due June 22, including backend and frontend deployment, ALB SSL configuration, load testing, optimization, and final deployment (2024-06-22; 1 day after June 21). Sprint 9 was planned for June 22–July 5, with 40 hours for bug fixes and 24 hours for documentation (13 calendar days between dates; 14 days inclusive). rollups.topic: Deployment milestones, estimates, and schedule changes

rollups.text: Jamie described a real-time trade-logging pipeline using Kafka 3.4.0 and Elasticsearch 8.5.1, with topic trade_events and index trade_logs (2024-07-06). A test of 10,000 simulated AAPL trades achieved 99.99% event-delivery success, while Jamie sought durability and fault tolerance (2024-07-06). Jamie also worked on indexing failures, circuit breaking, Prometheus/Grafana monitoring, Kafka Manager 3.0.0 connectivity to Amazon MSK, consumer timeouts, and Kafka ingestion performance (2024-07-06). Jamie reported reducing ingestion latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds after tuning batch size and compression (2024-07-06); further optimization and production monitoring remained topics of discussion. The records describe activity within the same date, with no elapsed calendar days between these steps.

Jamie repeatedly explored a circuit breaker for trading failures. On 2024-06-22, Jamie asked about halting live trading after five consecutive order failures in a 10-minute window and manually resetting the breaker before the window expired; the example used a 600-second timeout and reset cleared failures (2024-06-22). Jamie also explored fallback from Alpaca live trading to paper trading, including what to do if paper trading failed (2024-06-22). On 2024-07-06, Jamie again sought a breaker for five consecutive failures within 10 minutes, but the proposed implementation did not correctly enforce the rolling window (14 days after June 22). No production adoption is recorded.

Jamie repeatedly investigated Redis caching and invalidation: a 12-hour TTL to reduce database queries (2024-06-08); cache-aside behavior, cache misses, and invalidation after updates (2024-06-08); user-data caching with a three-node Redis cluster, one-hour TTL, and invalidation (2024-06-22); and caching query results to optimize PostgreSQL lookups (2024-06-22). Jamie also considered combining Redis with Memcached; the guidance favored Redis alone for the described user-data use case (2024-06-22).

Jamie asked about circuit breakers for trading order failures at least three times: a five-failure threshold within 10 minutes and manual reset (2024-06-22); live-to-paper fallback and paper API failure handling (2024-06-22); and a five-failure, 10-minute trading breaker (2024-07-06). These were requests for designs and examples; the records do not establish that a breaker was deployed.

Jamie reported two distinct trade-pipeline performance outcomes: the Kafka log-ingestion latency was reduced from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds after batch-size and compression tuning (2024-07-06); and a full trading-bot test of 1,000 trades over 24 hours achieved 98% successful execution (2024-07-06). These are different measurements and should not be treated as the same success metric.

Jamie’s planned production and project work included multiple estimates that changed or conflicted: 16 hours for final deployment and monitoring by June 21 (2024-06-08); 20 hours of listed tasks, or 22 with a proposed buffer, with a 16-hour reduced scope suggested (2024-06-08); 64 hours for Sprint 9 bug fixes and documentation through July 5 (2024-06-22); and a later estimate of about 14 hours for bug fixes and documentation by July 5 (2024-06-22). The records do not establish that the plans were completed on those dates.

Jamie’s trade-logging system: On 2024-07-06, Jamie described a Kafka-to-Elasticsearch pipeline and sought help with throughput, latency, error handling, scalability, test data, shard allocation, pagination, security, and production readiness. The documented setup used Kafka topic and Elasticsearch index `trade_logs`; Jamie also reported completed architecture diagrams and runbooks, and a time-series-oriented trade-log mapping. On 2024-07-07, Jamie approved the trade logging module for production release. Elapsed time from the documented project work on July 6 to approval was 1 day.

Jamie’s cursor-pagination work for Flask `GET /api/tradelogs`: On 2024-07-06, Jamie asked for help implementing cursor-based pagination. The proposed deterministic ascending-timestamp approach used a composite `(timestamp, id)` cursor, ordering by both fields and using the unique ID as a tie-breaker. Follow-up examples accepted `cursor` and `limit` and returned `data` and `next_cursor`, but did not establish robust cursor encoding and included an undefined `_limit` in one route. Later that day, Jamie asked about reducing endpoint latency; the conversation also covered indexing, caching, keyset pagination, profiling, and connection pooling. Elapsed time between these steps was 0 days.

Jamie’s mutual-TLS setup for Kafka: On 2024-07-06, Jamie asked how to enforce mutual TLS for microservices connecting to Kafka. The guidance covered broker SSL listeners, a server keystore, trusted client CA, `ssl.client.auth=required`, and client certificates and truststores. Jamie then asked whether both client and broker configuration needed updating; follow-ups reiterated that client keystore/truststore paths and passwords must be correct and brokers must be configured for SSL and restarted. Jamie also requested a Java producer example for `localhost:9092` and topic `tradelogs`. These steps all occurred on the same day.

Kafka topics and related trade-streaming uses mentioned by Jamie: `my_topic` for Kafka-to-Elasticsearch ingestion and test data (2024-07-06); `trade_logs` for the documented trade-logging pipeline and architecture (2024-07-06); `trade_execution_topic` for asynchronous trade-execution and analytics microservices (2024-07-06); and `tradelogs` in a requested Java mutual-TLS producer example (2024-07-06).

Jamie requested follow-up guidance about Kafka mutual TLS at least three times on 2024-07-06: the initial enforcement question, a question about updating client and broker configuration (with repeated follow-up exchanges), and a request for a Java producer example. The records document repeated discussion, not separate completed implementations.

Jamie asked for help with Kafka performance, scalability, or ingestion latency in at least four distinct recorded discussions on 2024-07-06: optimizing an MSK cluster, scaling Kafka-to-Elasticsearch trade ingestion, optimizing asynchronous trade-service communication, and reducing Kafka-to-Elasticsearch ingestion latency. These were separate requests on the same date.

Jamie’s production-readiness planning: On 2024-07-06, Jamie said final production deployment and monitoring were due 2024-07-10 and requested a sprint plan and task estimates. A separate request that day asked for a breakdown to complete production monitoring and documentation by 2024-07-10. The proposed schedules covered bug fixes, documentation, monitoring, security hardening, code review, release preparation, and final review. No later completion of the deployment or monitoring is recorded. From the planning date to the stated deadline was 4 days.
